headline_marked: [[France approves $11.2 billion internet tax]] based on traffic usage, costing $0.06 per gigabyte
headline: France approves $11.2 billion internet tax based on traffic usage, costing $0.06 per gigabyte
summary: French lawmakers have approved a new tax on internet data traffic, estimated to generate €10 billion ($11.2 billion) annually by charging content providers €0.055 ($0.06) per gigabyte.
details: French lawmakers have approved a new internet tax targeting major content providers like Google, Netflix, TikTok, and Meta. The proposed levy, passed by an 11-10 vote, will charge €0.055 (roughly $0.06) for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users. This tax is projected to generate approximately €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in annual revenue for the government.

The amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, aims at companies that generate substantial internet traffic rather than taxing advertising revenue or subscriptions. Google, Meta, Netflix, Amazon, and Akamai are specifically mentioned as major potential contributors, with TikTok also falling under the broader scope.

Internet service providers (ISPs) such as Orange, Free, and Liad will be responsible for measuring data volume and identifying the content providers. This data will then be collected quarterly and submitted to France's tax administration, overseen by the telecommunications watchdog Arcep.

To prevent excessive charges, the proposal includes a cap: the tax cannot exceed 15% of a company's French revenue or 2% of its worldwide revenue. It also accounts for content delivery networks (CDNs), which optimize content delivery but contribute to overall traffic.

Lhardit argues that the tax will primarily affect global technology companies, which account for about half of the 200 billion GB of data passing through French ISPs annually. He also disputes claims that costs would be passed on to users, citing free services like Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok as examples.

Opponents, including Government Minister David Amiel, raise concerns about user privacy and the complexity of measuring and attributing internet traffic without extensive monitoring. There are also worries about potential negative consequences for French businesses, though Lhardit suggests costs for local companies would be modest.

This move follows other European countries implementing digital service taxes, typically based on revenue. Meta, for instance, announced location-based fees for advertisers in several countries, including France, starting from July 1, 2026, to offset such levies.

headline_marked: [[Apple Maps]] now blurs sensitive NASA and military bases
headline: Apple Maps now blurs sensitive NASA and military bases
summary: Apple has begun blurring satellite imagery for several NASA facilities and U.S. military bases, including Space Force and Air Force installations, to enhance privacy and security.
details: Apple Maps is now obscuring satellite views of sensitive government locations, including NASA's Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, as well as various U.S. Air Force bases.
This move aims to bolster privacy and security for these critical facilities by making their detailed satellite imagery inaccessible through Apple's mapping service.
Previously, users could zoom in on these locations to see detailed infrastructure, launchpads, and operational areas. Now, these areas are presented with a blurred effect.
The change was first noticed by users exploring aerial views of Florida's space coast and has since been confirmed to apply to other military installations across the United States.
